answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — actually Dr. John Trainer
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in none of Lewis’s books, essays, or letters, and the C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it among quotations wrongly pinned to him. C.S. Lewis quote-researchers instead credit Dr. John Trainer, who says he coined it and shared it in a Facebook conversation on 30 December 2012 — and provided documentation of his authorship.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: Children are not a distraction from more important work. They are the most important work.
trail: The specialist project Essential C.S. Lewis flatly states the line is not by Lewis and credits Dr. John Trainer, who provided proof he coined it and shared it in a Facebook chat on 30 December 2012.
The fact-check blog Fauxtations found no primary source in Lewis’s books, Wikiquote, or Google Books — and gives “the nod to Dr. Trainer” absent any earlier citation.
The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it among quotations misattributed to Lewis, noting none of them were actually written by him.
source.excerptNote: A warm, aphoristic line beloved on motherhood and parenting merchandise — but not traceable to any book, essay, or letter by C.S. Lewis.

sourceLink.text: Essential C.S. Lewis: the “Children Distraction” investigation

source.rightsNote: The wording is a modern coinage, first documented in a 30 December 2012 Facebook post by Dr. John Trainer, and so is treated as in copyright to its author under U.S. rules for works published in or after 1931. (It was never a C.S. Lewis text at all.)

author.name: Dr. John Trainer
author.heading: About Dr. John Trainer
author.metaLine: Coined the line in 2012 · credited originator per C.S. Lewis quote researchers
author.bio: Dr. John Trainer is credited by C.S. Lewis quote-researchers as the person who actually coined this line, having shared it in a Facebook conversation on 30 December 2012 and later supplied documentation of his authorship. Beyond that origin story, little is publicly recorded about him — but the specialist projects that track fake Lewis quotes give him the nod for the wording that the internet later re-pinned onto Lewis.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misattribution: a feel-good, quotable line stuck onto C.S. Lewis, whose fame lends it instant authority. It appears in none of his writing.

items.why: The line is absent from Lewis’s books, essays, and letters. The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists it among quotes misattributed to him, and Fauxtations found no primary source for it in Lewis’s writing.

items.who: “On Three Ways of Writing for Children”
items.why: Some sharers claimed the line came from Lewis’s 1952 talk on writing for children, but Fauxtations checked that essay and found the quotation is simply not in it.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording traces to Dr. John Trainer, who documented coining it and sharing it on Facebook on 30 December 2012, per Essential C.S. Lewis.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The sentiment — that raising children is not a detour from meaningful work but the meaning of it — lands hard with parents, and it reads exactly like the kind of gentle, moral aphorism people expect from the author of the Narnia books and Mere Christianity. That plausibility is precisely what makes the misattribution stick.
The line proliferated on nursery prints, motherhood merchandise, and social posts, almost always over Lewis’s name. Even Focus on the Family reportedly credited it to Lewis on Facebook.
context.pull: It sounds like Lewis. That’s exactly why it isn’t.
